primary_cause: Surprise CEO transition: Bob Iger replaced by Bob Chapek Feb 25-26. Needham questioned Chapek's content experience
secondary_factors: Growing fear that COVID would materially hit parks cruises and theatrical operations
store_description: Reuters said Disney shares fell about 2% in premarket on Feb 26 after the succession surprise with Needham explicitly questioning Chapek's content background. On Feb 27 investors still were not convinced as the stock closed down while Chapek confronted possible coronavirus damage to parks and films.

primary_cause: Broad equity de-risking tied to COVID panic
secondary_factors: Utilities were defensive but indiscriminate selling still hit rate-sensitive sectors during forced liquidation
store_description: By Feb 27 markets were in a rapid correction as coronavirus spread beyond China. Duke's drop does not appear tied to company news. It looks much more like a macro risk-off move.

primary_cause: Broad market selloff tied to coronavirus growth fears
secondary_factors: Concern that global lab/industrial activity and cross-border supply chains would be disrupted
store_description: No strong evidence of a Danaher-specific catalyst. Investors were aggressively repricing global growth and supply-chain-sensitive businesses. Danaher fell less than many cyclicals.

primary_cause: Broad market liquidation not Costco fundamentals
secondary_factors: Reuters Feb 28 described consumers beginning to hoard staples with Costco as key example. Demand actually improving
store_description: Costco's own near-term setup was arguably improving because panic buying was starting. The Feb 27 decline looks less like company trouble and more like indiscriminate market selling during the COVID correction.

primary_cause: Collapsing rates and margin fears for banks. Powell issued rare Feb 28 statement to act as appropriate
secondary_factors: Recession/credit-loss fears as coronavirus spread globally. 10yr Treasury plunging
store_description: For banks this week's selloff directly threatened earnings power because net interest margins compress when the curve collapses. With the 10-year Treasury plunging and the market pricing emergency easing JPM sold off as investors marked down 2020 profitability.

primary_cause: Falling yields and worsening bank earnings expectations. Powell act as appropriate
secondary_factors: Broader risk-off selling and concern over credit quality in a COVID slowdown
store_description: Wells was already a margin-sensitive bank with less strategic flexibility. The rapid move in rates was especially damaging to sentiment. Powell's statement effectively confirmed the policy pivot markets feared.

primary_cause: Broad market selloff. Indiscriminate selling despite utilities defensive profile
secondary_factors: Portfolio de-risking. Utilities normally benefit from lower rates so 4% drop suggests forced selling
store_description: Southern's decline was not supported by a clear company event. It was more a symptom of the late-February market panic. A nearly 4% drop in a utility suggests forced selling and index-level risk reduction.

primary_cause: Broad COVID selloff
secondary_factors: Concern over global consumption and away-from-home channels
store_description: Pepsi did not appear to have a stock-specific negative catalyst. The stock's decline looks tied to the market's rapid repricing of global consumer demand and supply-chain risk.

primary_cause: Prior Jan 29 coronavirus revenue warning getting repriced more aggressively as outbreak spread. China ~4.5% of sales. 2 factories closed
secondary_factors: Broad market selloff and concern about Asian exposure/supply chains
store_description: Mondelez had already quantified the issue: Q1 revenue would be hit two factories were closed and China represented about 4.5% of sales. When the market realized the virus was becoming a global problem investors had a concrete reason to discount Mondelez more aggressively.

primary_cause: Fear that COVID would move from China issue to broader global restaurant traffic issue. Had closed several hundred of ~3,300 China outlets
secondary_factors: Overall market selloff and concern about international exposure especially in Asia and eventually Europe
store_description: Earlier management messaging assumed the effect would stay modest if the virus remained largely in China but the late-February global spread undermined that assumption. Investors likely repriced McDonald's on the view that international restaurant traffic and franchise economics would weaken beyond China.

primary_cause: Broad market selloff. Defense names sold in broad risk-off
secondary_factors: De-risking across industrial and aerospace baskets
store_description: No compelling evidence of a company-specific trigger for Lockheed right before Feb 28. The drop looks like index and sector contagion rather than a reassessment of defense demand or contract flow.

primary_cause: Broad market selloff. Portfolio liquidation even in defensive healthcare
secondary_factors: Not a discrete new litigation or earnings event
store_description: J&J usually acts defensively so a 3.3% decline suggests investors were selling almost everything during the late-February panic. No specific J&J corporate development was the main driver.

primary_cause: Broad market selloff overwhelming POSITIVE stock-specific news. Feb 26 announced two Phase 3 remdesivir studies ~1,000 patients
secondary_factors: Uncertainty over whether remdesivir would ultimately work plus biotech volatility during correction
store_description: Gilead had a real catalyst but it was favorable: two global Phase 3 remdesivir studies. The stock still fell 4.5% which strongly suggests the market-wide COVID panic and de-risking outweighed the upside optionality from remdesivir at that point.

primary_cause: Broad market selloff. Defense/industrial baskets
secondary_factors: Concern that business-jet and IT activity could weaken if COVID triggered recession
store_description: Not enough evidence for a clean company-specific catalyst. Likeliest explanation is macro de-risking with some added sensitivity because Gulfstream/business aviation would later prove exposed.

primary_cause: Continuing broad market liquidation. Second straight day of decline
secondary_factors: Indiscriminate selling despite lower-rate tailwinds for utilities
store_description: Duke's second straight decline looks like part of the same macro wave rather than a new company development.

primary_cause: Marketwide selling not Costco-specific deterioration. Reuters showed hoarding lines at Costco — operationally favorable
secondary_factors: Investors selling even perceived winners during forced unwinds
store_description: Costco was arguably one of the few retailers seeing immediate demand upside from pandemic preparations with Reuters documenting lines and stocking-up behavior. The fact that the stock still dropped 4.1% tells you this was mainly a liquidity and correlation event.

primary_cause: Broad market selloff. Global sourcing/exposure concern
secondary_factors: Consumer staples with global sourcing still faced supply-chain disruption fears
store_description: Colgate's decline appears macro rather than company-specific. The market was repricing even defensive staples for global logistics and demand uncertainty.

primary_cause: Worsening commercial aviation outlook from COVID layered onto 737 MAX crisis. Airlines extending China/HK cancellations through April
secondary_factors: IATA warned 4.7% demand decline first time in 11 years. Ongoing MAX overhang and cash-flow strain
store_description: Boeing was uniquely vulnerable because COVID hit the same end market already weakened by the MAX grounding. As airlines cut routes and industry demand forecasts rolled over investors had concrete reason to assume further delivery pressure weaker orders and more cash-flow strain.

primary_cause: Broad market selloff. Enterprise consulting/project demand concern
secondary_factors: Risk to consulting spend travel-heavy project work and discretionary IT programs
store_description: No strong evidence of a discrete Accenture event. Investors discounting a possible pause in corporate transformation spending as clients dealt with coronavirus disruption and recession risk.

primary_cause: Broad market selloff. Smaller decline than cyclicals
secondary_factors: Worry that worsening outbreak could hit discretionary foot traffic and housing-related demand
store_description: This looks mostly macro. Home Depot's decline was smaller than many cyclical names which fits the idea that investors were reducing exposure broadly rather than reacting to a company-specific warning.
